sets.title: Non-defining relative clauses
sets.task: Combine the facts into ONE sentence. Add the extra information with a relative clause, put between commas.
sets.formula: Main noun, which / who / whose + extra information, + rest of the sentence.
sets.hint: Choose one fact as the main message. Turn the other into ", which ..." or ", who ..." and place it straight after the noun it describes. Commas on both sides, unless the clause ends the sentence.

facts: Tokyo is the capital of Japan.
Tokyo has more than thirty million residents in its wider area.
checks: a relative clause after a comma (, which / , who / , whose)
items.model: Tokyo, which is the capital of Japan, has more than thirty million residents in its wider area.

facts: The Nile is the longest river in Africa.
The Nile flows through eleven countries.
checks: a relative clause after a comma (, which / , who / , whose)
items.model: The Nile, which is the longest river in Africa, flows through eleven countries.

facts: Dr Amina Rahimova led the study.
She works at the University of Tashkent.
checks: a relative clause after a comma (, which / , who / , whose)
items.model: The study, which surveyed 2,000 students, was led by Dr Amina Rahimova, who works at the University of Tashkent.

facts: Solar power is now the cheapest source of electricity in many regions.
Solar power was considered too expensive twenty years ago.
checks: a relative clause after a comma (, which / , who / , whose)
items.model: Solar power, which was considered too expensive twenty years ago, is now the cheapest source of electricity in many regions.

facts: The government introduced a congestion charge in 2019.
The congestion charge reduced traffic in the city centre by 15 per cent.
checks: a relative clause after a comma (, which / , who / , whose)
items.model: The government introduced a congestion charge in 2019, which reduced traffic in the city centre by 15 per cent.

sets.title: Participle clauses
sets.task: Combine the facts into ONE sentence. Open with, or end with, a participle clause (-ing or -ed).
sets.formula: V-ing / V-ed ..., main clause.   OR   Main clause, V-ing (result).
sets.hint: Take the first action and make it the opener: "Facing ...", "Built in ...", "Having studied ...". The subject of the main clause must be the same person or thing. For a result, end with ", leading to ..." or ", causing ...".

checks: a participle clause: an opening -ing/-ed phrase followed by a comma, or a ", -ing" result clause
items.model: Facing rising costs, the company moved production abroad.

facts: The bridge still carries 40,000 vehicles a day.
checks: a participle clause: an opening -ing/-ed phrase followed by a comma, or a ", -ing" result clause
items.model: Built in 1932, the bridge still carries 40,000 vehicles a day.

facts: Many students have studied online since 2020.
Many students now prefer flexible timetables.
checks: a participle clause: an opening -ing/-ed phrase followed by a comma, or a ", -ing" result clause
items.model: Having studied online since 2020, many students now prefer flexible timetables.

facts: Fuel prices led to higher food prices.
checks: a participle clause: an opening -ing/-ed phrase followed by a comma, or a ", -ing" result clause
items.model: Fuel prices rose sharply, leading to higher food prices.

facts: The council introduced free bus travel for pensioners.
The council hoped to reduce loneliness.
checks: a participle clause: an opening -ing/-ed phrase followed by a comma, or a ", -ing" result clause
items.model: Introducing free bus travel for pensioners, the council hoped to reduce loneliness.

sets.title: The semicolon
sets.task: Join the two facts into ONE sentence with a semicolon. Do not use and, but or so after it.
sets.hint: A semicolon replaces a full stop between two complete sentences that are closely linked in meaning. Both halves must be able to stand alone. A linking adverb such as "however" may follow it.

facts: Public transport is cheaper and cleaner.
checks: a semicolon between two clauses, with no and / but / or / so straight after it
items.model: Cars are convenient; public transport, however, is cheaper and cleaner.

facts: Others learn better from group projects.
checks: a semicolon between two clauses, with no and / but / or / so straight after it
items.model: Some students prefer lectures; others learn better from group projects.

facts: Imports fell in the same year.
checks: a semicolon between two clauses, with no and / but / or / so straight after it
items.model: Exports rose in 2018; imports, in contrast, fell in the same year.

facts: The experiment was repeated three times.
The results were consistent each time.
checks: a semicolon between two clauses, with no and / but / or / so straight after it
items.model: The experiment was repeated three times; the results were consistent each time.

facts: Renewable energy is expensive to install.
It is cheap to run for decades.
checks: a semicolon between two clauses, with no and / but / or / so straight after it
items.model: Renewable energy is expensive to install; it is cheap to run for decades.

sets.title: The colon
sets.task: Write ONE sentence that uses a colon to introduce the explanation or list.
sets.formula: Complete clause: explanation, example or list.
sets.hint: Say the full general statement first. Then put the colon and the specific detail. Never put a colon straight after a verb such as "is" or "include".

facts: The factors are cost, distance and time.
checks: a colon after a full clause, followed by the detail
no colon straight after a verb such as is / are / include
items.model: Three factors explain the decline: cost, distance and time.

facts: The city has one major problem.
checks: a colon after a full clause, followed by the detail
no colon straight after a verb such as is / are / include
items.model: The city has one major problem: housing.

facts: They can raise taxes on fuel.
checks: a colon after a full clause, followed by the detail
no colon straight after a verb such as is / are / include
items.model: Governments can take two actions: they can raise taxes on fuel or invest in rail.

facts: The survey produced a clear result.
checks: a colon after a full clause, followed by the detail
no colon straight after a verb such as is / are / include
items.model: The survey produced a clear result: most respondents distrust online reviews.

facts: Education should be free at every level.
checks: a colon after a full clause, followed by the detail
no colon straight after a verb such as is / are / include
items.model: The writer makes one argument: education should be free at every level.

sets.title: Contrast and concession
sets.task: Combine the facts into ONE sentence that shows contrast. Use although, while, whereas or despite. Do not use "but".
sets.formula: Although + clause, main clause.   Clause, whereas / while + clause.   Despite + noun / -ing, main clause.
sets.hint: Put the less important or expected idea in the although-clause. Use a comma between the two parts. Never use "although" and "but" together.

facts: Many people still drive to work.
checks: a contrast word: although, though, while, whilst, whereas or despite
a comma between the two parts
items.model: Although cycling is healthy, many people still drive to work.

checks: a contrast word: although, though, while, whilst, whereas or despite
a comma between the two parts
items.model: Urban populations are growing quickly, whereas rural populations are shrinking.

facts: It reduces the income of local shops.
checks: a contrast word: although, though, while, whilst, whereas or despite
a comma between the two parts
items.model: While online shopping is convenient, it reduces the income of local shops.

facts: It raised a large amount of money.
checks: a contrast word: although, though, while, whilst, whereas or despite
a comma between the two parts
items.model: Despite being unpopular, the new tax raised a large amount of money.

facts: Salaries in the city are higher.
The cost of living is also higher.
checks: uses the information: cost of living
a contrast word: although, though, while, whilst, whereas or despite
a comma between the two parts
items.model: Although salaries in the city are higher, the cost of living is also higher.

sets.title: Conditionals: types 1, 2 and 3
sets.task: Write ONE conditional sentence of the type named. Mixed conditionals are not allowed.
sets.formula: Type 1: If + present, will + verb.   Type 2: If + past, would + verb.   Type 3: If + had + V3, would have + V3.
sets.hint: Type 1 is a real possibility. Type 2 is unreal or unlikely now. Type 3 is a past situation that cannot be changed. Check the verb forms on BOTH sides of the sentence.

checks: first conditional: if + present, will + verb
items.task: Write a FIRST conditional sentence (real future possibility).
items.model: If the government subsidises solar panels, more households will install them.

facts: Cities may build more cycle lanes.
checks: first conditional: if + present, will + verb
items.task: Write a FIRST conditional sentence (real future possibility).
items.model: If cities build more cycle lanes, fewer people will drive.

facts: Schools do not teach financial skills.
Many young adults get into debt.
checks: second conditional: if + past, would + verb
items.task: Write a SECOND conditional sentence (unreal or unlikely now).
items.model: If schools taught financial skills, fewer young adults would get into debt.

checks: second conditional: if + past, would + verb
items.task: Write a SECOND conditional sentence (unreal or unlikely now).
items.model: If tickets were cheaper, more people would attend live concerts.

facts: Hundreds of workers lost their jobs.
checks: third conditional: if + had + V3, would have + V3
items.task: Write a THIRD conditional sentence (past situation that cannot change).
items.model: If the factory had not closed in 2010, hundreds of workers would not have lost their jobs.

facts: The city did not invest in flood defences.
checks: third conditional: if + had + V3, would have + V3
items.task: Write a THIRD conditional sentence (past situation that cannot change).
items.model: If the city had invested in flood defences, the 2021 floods would not have caused such severe damage.

sets.title: Passive and impersonal structures
sets.task: Rewrite the information using the structure named. No person or group may be the subject.
sets.formula: It is believed / estimated that ...   X is thought to ...   X was built / has been discovered ...
sets.hint: Make the thing affected the subject. Use be + past participle. Drop "people", "scientists" or "someone" unless the doer really matters.

facts: People widely believe that sleep improves memory.
checks: impersonal passive (it is believed / thought / estimated that ..., or is thought to ...)
items.task: Use an impersonal passive: "It is believed that ..." or "X is thought to ...".
items.model: It is widely believed that sleep improves memory.

facts: Researchers estimate that 70 per cent of plastic is not recycled.
checks: impersonal passive (it is estimated / believed / thought that ...)
items.task: Use an impersonal passive: "It is estimated that ...".
items.model: It is estimated that 70 per cent of plastic is not recycled.

facts: Nobody has used the stadium since 2019.
checks: a present perfect passive: has not been used / has been unused
items.task: Write ONE sentence with two passive verbs and no doer.
items.model: The stadium was built in 2015 but has not been used since 2019.

facts: Scientists have discovered a new species of frog in Peru.
Nobody had seen the frog before 2022.
checks: a past perfect or past passive: had not been seen / was not seen
items.task: Write ONE sentence with two passive verbs and no doer.
items.model: A new species of frog has been discovered in Peru; it had not been seen before 2022.

facts: Teachers should give students more time to revise.
items.task: Use a passive with "should": make "students" the subject.
items.model: Students should be given more time to revise.

sets.title: Inversion for emphasis
sets.task: Rewrite the information as ONE sentence that begins with the negative or limiting expression named. The auxiliary verb comes BEFORE the subject.
sets.formula: Not only + auxiliary + subject ..., but ... also.   Rarely / Never + auxiliary + subject.   Only by + -ing + auxiliary + subject.   No sooner had + subject + V3 than ...
sets.hint: After the fronted expression the word order becomes question order: auxiliary, then subject, then verb. "Rarely do governments admit", not "Rarely governments admit".

checks: begins "Not only" + auxiliary (do / does / is / are ...)
items.task: Begin with "Not only".
items.model: Not only do smartphones help people to communicate, but they also damage concentration.

items.task: Begin with "Rarely" or "Seldom".
items.model: Rarely do governments admit mistakes.

facts: Students can succeed only by working consistently.
checks: begins "Only by ..." and then a verb before the subject (can / do / will)
items.task: Begin with "Only by".
items.model: Only by working consistently can students succeed.

facts: As soon as the results were published, the public demanded action.
checks: no sooner had ... than  /  hardly had ... when
items.task: Use "No sooner" or "Hardly".
items.model: No sooner had the results been published than the public demanded action.

facts: The company had never faced such a crisis.
checks: begins Never / Little + had / has / did
items.task: Begin with "Never" or "Little".
items.model: Never had the company faced such a crisis.

sets.title: Nominalisation
sets.task: Express the same idea in ONE sentence whose subject is a noun phrase (a rise in ..., the expansion of ...). Do not use because, so or as a result.
sets.formula: A rise in X led to a fall in Y.   The expansion of X resulted in the loss of Y.   Increased X has placed pressure on Y.
sets.hint: Turn each verb into a noun: rose to a rise, expanded to expansion, spent to spending, invest to investment. Then link the two noun phrases with a verb such as led to, resulted in, caused or placed.

facts: As a result, people spent less.
checks: no 'because', 'so' or 'as a result': the noun phrase must do the linking
noun phrase: a rise / increase in unemployment
noun phrase: a fall / drop / decline in spending
items.model: A rise in unemployment led to a fall in consumer spending.

checks: no 'because', 'so' or 'as a result': the noun phrase must do the linking
noun phrase: the expansion / growth of cities
noun phrase: the loss / disappearance of farmland
items.model: The rapid expansion of cities resulted in the loss of farmland.

facts: So health services face greater demand.
checks: no 'because', 'so' or 'as a result': the noun phrase must do the linking
noun phrase: life expectancy / longer lives / longevity
items.model: Increased life expectancy has placed greater demand on health services.

checks: no 'because', 'so' or 'as a result': the noun phrase must do the linking
items.model: Widespread cheating among students is a concern for universities.

checks: no 'because', 'so' or 'as a result': the noun phrase must do the linking
reduced pollution / a reduction in pollution / lower pollution
items.model: Investment in public transport by governments leads to reduced pollution.

sets.title: Cleft sentences
sets.task: Rewrite the idea as ONE cleft sentence using the pattern named.
sets.formula: It is / was + focus + that / who ...   What + subject + verb + is / was ...
sets.hint: A cleft sentence pushes the important word to the front. "It is poor diet that causes ..." focuses on diet. "What governments need to do is ..." focuses on the action.

facts: Poor diet causes most health problems, not lack of exercise.
items.task: Use "It is ... that".
items.model: It is poor diet, not lack of exercise, that causes most health problems.

items.task: Use "It is ... who".
items.model: It is teachers who influence students most strongly.

facts: The invention of the printing press changed European society.
items.task: Use "It was ... that".
items.model: It was the invention of the printing press that changed European society.

facts: Governments need to act on emissions.
items.task: Use "What ... is".
items.model: What governments need to do is to act on emissions.

facts: Young people were most affected by the 2008 crisis.
items.task: Use "It was ... who".
items.model: It was young people who were most affected by the 2008 crisis.

sets.title: Cause and result
sets.task: Combine the facts into ONE sentence, showing cause and result with the structure named.
sets.formula: so + adjective + that   /   such + noun phrase + that   /   , leading to + noun   /   as a result of + noun phrase
sets.hint: so + adjective + that + result.  such a / such + noun + that + result.  Main clause, resulting in + noun.  Result + as a result of + noun phrase (not a clause).

items.task: Use "so ... that".
items.model: The exam was so difficult that half of the candidates failed.

facts: There was a huge rise in demand.
items.task: Use "such ... that".
items.model: There was such a huge rise in demand that supplies ran out within days.

checks: leading to / resulting in / leads to / results in
\b(leading to|resulting in|leads to|results in|contributing to|giving rise to)\b
items.task: Use "leading to" or "resulting in" followed by a noun phrase.
items.model: Deforestation destroys habitats, resulting in the extinction of many species.

checks: as a result of / owing to / due to / because of
\b(as a result of|owing to|due to|because of|on account of)\b
items.task: Use "as a result of", "owing to" or "due to" followed by a NOUN PHRASE.
items.model: Harvests failed as a result of a sharp decrease in rainfall.

checks: a semicolon, then consequently / therefore / thus / as a result
items.task: Join with a semicolon and a result adverb (consequently, therefore, thus).
items.model: The company cut prices; consequently, sales doubled.

sets.title: Task 1: comparing figures
sets.task: Write ONE sentence that compares or describes the figures, using the language named. The figures are exact: do not distort them.
sets.formula: doubled / tripled   three times as many / much as   half that of   almost / approximately / just over
sets.hint: Check the arithmetic before you write. 20 to 40 is a doubling. 60 against 20 is three times. 25 against 50 is half. Use "as many as" with countable nouns and "as much as" with uncountable ones.

items.task: Show that the figure doubled.
items.model: Sales doubled from 20 million units in 2010 to 40 million units in 2020.

facts: Country A: 60 units of energy per person.
Country B: 20 units of energy per person.
items.task: Show that A is three times B.
items.model: Country A used three times as much energy per person as Country B.

checks: half that / half the / half as many / twice as many (men)
items.task: Show the relationship with "half".
items.model: In 2000, the proportion of women who smoked was half that of men.

items.task: Use an approximation word: almost, nearly, approximately, roughly or just under.
items.model: Prices rose by almost 50 per cent, from $100 to $149.

checks: a multiple: twice / double / two times
items.task: Use an approximation word AND a multiple.
items.model: Group Y had approximately twice as many students as Group X.

sets.title: Apposition (extra noun phrase in commas)
sets.task: Combine the facts into ONE sentence. Give the extra information as a noun phrase between commas, with no verb of its own after the noun.
sets.formula: Subject, a / an / the + noun phrase, verb ...
sets.hint: Repeat nothing. The second fact becomes a description of the subject: "Dr Chen, a leading economist, argues ...". Two commas wrap the description.

Dr Chen argues that wages must rise.
checks: an appositive noun phrase between commas (, a / an / the ... ,)
items.model: Dr Chen, a leading economist, argues that wages must rise.

items.model: Plastic, a material that takes centuries to decompose, is used in most packaging.

facts: Mobile banking is a rapid change in how people manage money.

checks: an appositive noun phrase between commas (, a / an / the ... ,)

sets.title: Introductions
sets.task: Write the INTRODUCTION: 2 or 3 sentences. Sentence 1 paraphrases the topic in your own words. The next sentence (or two) gives your position or says exactly what the essay will do. Do not copy five words in a row from the question.
sets.why: A Band 9 introduction does two jobs and nothing else: it restates the topic without copying, and it commits to a clear plan or position. No background story, no famous quotations.

sets.title: Conclusions

sets.title: Body paragraphs
sets.task: Write ONE full body paragraph (75 to 140 words, at least four sentences): a clear topic sentence, an explanation, ONE specific example, and a closing sentence that links back to the idea.
sets.why: Most candidates write a paragraph with an idea but no development. A Band 9 paragraph moves from claim to explanation to example to consequence, and uses cautious language where certainty would be false.

items.idea: Public transport reduces air pollution in large cities.
support: One bus or train carries many passengers.
Fewer private cars burn fuel.
Example: a city opens a new metro line.
checks: an example marker (For example, For instance, such as, a case in point, Consider ...)
\b(for example|for instance|such as|a case in point|consider|to illustrate)\b

a cause or result link (because, so, as a result, therefore, which ...)

items.model: Public transport can significantly reduce air pollution in large cities. A single bus or train carriage can carry the passengers of dozens of private cars, so fewer vehicles are burning fuel on the roads. For example, when a city opens a new metro line, many commuters tend to leave their cars at home, and traffic on parallel routes often falls. As a result, the concentration of harmful gases near busy streets may decrease, which benefits the health of residents, particularly children and older people.

items.model: Online courses offer students a level of flexibility that traditional classrooms rarely provide. Learners can study at times that suit their own routines, which is especially valuable for adults who combine education with full-time work. Consider a nurse who works night shifts: she could watch recorded lectures in the morning, whereas a fixed timetable would probably prevent her from attending at all. Consequently, online study may open higher education to people who would otherwise be excluded.

items.model: Harsher sentences do not always deter crime, because most offenders do not expect to be caught. For instance, a person who commits a robbery on impulse is unlikely to consider the length of a possible sentence, so the threat of ten years rather than five has little influence on behaviour. Evidence suggests that the certainty of being caught deters more effectively than the severity of punishment. Therefore, improving policing may achieve more than extending prison terms.

items.model: Working from home can weaken the sense of teamwork that develops naturally in an office. Colleagues who rarely meet face to face tend to communicate only about tasks, so informal conversations that build trust and generate ideas become less frequent. For example, a new employee who joins a remote team may struggle to learn unwritten rules or to find a mentor. Over time, this isolation can reduce motivation and may even lead talented staff to leave.

items.model: Mass tourism may damage local culture when traditions are adapted to please visitors rather than to serve the community. Ceremonies that once marked important moments in village life can become short performances staged daily for cameras. A case in point is a festival that is shortened and simplified so that tour groups can watch it between meals. As a result, younger residents may come to see their heritage as a product to be sold, which weakens its original meaning.

items.model: Free university education would widen access for talented students from poor families. When tuition fees are removed, young people no longer have to choose between a degree and a lifetime of debt, so ability rather than family income decides who studies. For instance, a gifted student from a low-income household might otherwise reject a place at a good university for fear of borrowing. Consequently, society could benefit from a wider pool of well-qualified doctors, engineers and teachers.

items.model: Reading for pleasure is one of the most effective ways to expand a person's vocabulary. Unlike a word list, a novel presents new words repeatedly and in context, so readers gradually absorb their meaning without deliberate effort. For example, a teenager who reads detective stories regularly will probably meet terms such as 'suspect' and 'motive' dozens of times. This repeated exposure helps the words to become part of the reader's active language, which is likely to improve both writing and speaking.

items.model: Living alone encourages independence, but it may also bring a risk of loneliness. Residents must manage every task themselves, from budgeting to cooking, and this responsibility often builds confidence and practical skills. However, the same freedom can mean long evenings without conversation. For example, an elderly person whose neighbours have moved away may go several days without speaking to anyone, which can affect both mood and health. Therefore, communities should create regular opportunities for single residents to meet.
